questions.question: An angle measures 145°. What type of angle is it?
questions.explain: An obtuse angle is bigger than 90° but smaller than 180°, and 145° fits there. A common trap is calling any 'big' angle reflex — reflex angles must be larger than 180°.

questions.question: Which of these angle measures is a reflex angle?
questions.explain: A reflex angle is more than 180° but less than 360°, so 240° is the only one. Watch out: 175° and 180° are still obtuse and straight, not reflex.

questions.question: A straight angle measures how many degrees?
questions.explain: A straight angle is a half turn, which is 180° — the two arms make one straight line. Many students mix this up with 360°, which is a full turn all the way around.

questions.question: Small Number builds a launch ramp at the skateboard park. The ramp meets the ground at 30°. What type of angle is 30°?
questions.explain: Any angle smaller than 90° is acute, so 30° is acute. A common mistake is thinking a small, sharp-looking angle is a right angle just because it is part of a ramp corner.

questions.question: Ayla looks at the corner of a kite flying at Spanish Banks. The corner is clearly bigger than a right angle, but nowhere near a straight angle. Using 45°, 90°, and 180° as reference angles, what is the best estimate?
questions.explain: Compare to the reference angles: bigger than 90° but far from 180° points to about 110°. The trap is picking 175°, which would look almost like a straight line, or 200°, which would bend backwards into a reflex angle.

questions.question: Two angles sit side by side along a straight edge of a park bench, so together they make a straight angle. One angle measures 65°. What does the other measure?
questions.explain: Angles on a straight line add to 180°, so 180° − 65° = 115°. The most common mistake is subtracting from 90° and getting 25°, which only works for angles inside a right angle.

questions.question: A triangular sign at the trailhead is an equilateral triangle, so its three angles are equal and add to 180°. What is each angle, and what type is it?
questions.explain: Divide first: 180° ÷ 3 = 60°, and 60° is less than 90°, so each angle is acute. A frequent slip is doubling instead of dividing and choosing 120°.

questions.question: The gate on a backyard fence swings open. The angle between the gate and the fence on the inside measures 100°. What is the reflex angle on the outside of the gate?
questions.explain: A full turn is 360°, so the reflex angle is 360° − 100° = 260°. Students often subtract from 180° and get 80°, but that gives the angle on a straight line, not the reflex angle going all the way around.

questions.question: Priya and Jayden each draw a 50° angle. Jayden draws his with arms 10 cm long; Priya draws hers with arms 3 cm long. Jayden says his angle is bigger. Who is correct?
options: Jayden is right — longer arms make a bigger angle.
Jayden is right — 10 cm + 50° is more than 3 cm + 50°.
Neither angle can be compared until the arms are the same length.
Priya is right — both angles are 50°, because angle size depends on the opening, not the arm length.
questions.explain: An angle measures how far one arm turns from the other, so the length of the arms changes nothing — both are 50°. This is the most common angle misconception: judging size by how long the lines look instead of how wide the opening is.

questions.question: A patio at a Kelowna community centre is paved with regular hexagon stones. The six interior angles of a hexagon add to 720°, and in a regular hexagon they are all equal. What is each interior angle, and what type of angle is it?
questions.explain: Divide 720° ÷ 6 = 120°, and since 120° is between 90° and 180°, it is obtuse. Two traps here: using 108° (that is a regular pentagon) and calling 120° reflex — reflex needs more than 180°.

questions.question: Small Number rolls into the skateboard bowl facing the fence. He turns 90° to the right, then keeps turning another 45° in the same direction. Measured from where he started, how far has he turned, and what type of angle is that?
questions.explain: Turns in the same direction add: 90° + 45° = 135°, which is between 90° and 180°, so it is obtuse. Common traps are subtracting the two turns instead of adding, or labelling 135° reflex because it sounds large.

questions.question: On the classroom clock, each hour mark is 30° from the next. At exactly 4:00, what is the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand, and what type of angle is it?
questions.explain: From 12 to 4 is 4 hour marks, so 4 × 30° = 120°, which is obtuse. The usual trap is measuring the long way around the clock face and answering 240° — the angle between the hands is the smaller opening unless the question asks for the reflex angle.
